full_judgment:
8. This was the legal scenario against which the Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty Act, 2012 ("the VAT and SD Act") came into force on 1-7-2019 by notification through SR0/168-Ain/2019/25-Mushak dated 13-6-2019. It is the petitioners' contention that this new piece of legislation endorses zero-rated VAT on the fees/ commission earned against services rendered by shipping agents through sections 21(1)(Ka) and 24(11)(Ka) and (Gha) read with section 2 (11) and (12). Simultaneously, the NBR in exercise of its power under section 32Ka of the VAT and SD Act issued SRO No. 186 Ain/2019/43-Mushak dated 13-6-2019 to determine the boundaries of taxable services and in that process provided further content to the scope and nature of shipping agent services under Service Code No. S035.00. In this regard, it is noted that vis-à-vis SRO No. 186 the petitioners' general stance has been of reliance on that Order to explain and delineate the periphery and limits to the notion of "shipping agents" as distinct and distinguishable from ancillary transport services defined in section 2(11) of the VAT and SD Act. The petitioners submit that as such the periphery and parameters of shipping agents' functions have been identified under Service Code No. S035.00 in a manner so as to wholly distinguish from the category of services defined as ancillary transport services under section 2(11) of the said Act and, as such, all BSAA members who render the services as explained in Service Code No. S035.00 as shipping agents are entitled to zero-rated VAT by operation of section 21(1)(Ka) and section 24(11)(Ka) of the VAT and SD Act. 

 9. It is deemed prudent at this juncture to reproduce for ease of reference the relevant provisions of law drawn from the VAT and SD Act, the Customs Act, 1969 the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 and other related pieces of legislation inclusive of the relevant part of the table in SRO No. 186 and these are, accordingly, extracted as hereunder:— 

 6. SRO No. 186 dated 13-6-2019 

 11. The factual trajectory thereafter leads to the refusal of the respondent No. 4, Second Secretary (VAT, Law and Rules), VAT Policy, NBR vide the impugned Memo dated 1-12-2020 to recognize that VAT on shipping agents' fees/commission shall be zero-rated. Notably, the respondent No. 5, BB followed suit and vide its letter dated 29-12-2020 informed BSAA that VAT shall be applicable on shipping agents' service fees/commission. The Court pauses here to reflect on the rationale behind this unfavourable stance taken by the NBR and the BB against the petitioners which, the petitioners argue, reflect a fundamental misunderstanding of the applicable provisions of the law both by the NBR and the BB. Both the impugned memos of 1-12-2020 and 29-12-2020 accept as their common baseline the explanation provided of the term "shipping agent" in SRO No. 186 of 13-6-2019. According to that explanation under Service Code No. 5035.00, as quoted earlier, a shipping agent means any person, entity or association engaged in conducting business related to the arrival, stay and departure of any "conveyance" defined under section 2(g) of the Customs Act, 1969 (i.e., any means of transport used for carrying goods such as a vessel). The said explanation also allows for any local agent of a foreign shipping line to be considered as a shipping agent for the purpose of identifying the extent and scope of taxable service. 

 21. In reply the petitioners present SRO No. 186 as drawing statutorily authorized boundaries of any taxable service and does so by drawing periphery and limits of the nature and scope of shipping agents' service under Service Code 5035.00 in a manner and with intent to set these apart from those that make up ancillary transport services stipulated in section 2(11) of the VAT and SD Act. 

 23. Upon a perusal of the pleadings and consideration of the submissions made by both sides this Court finds at the outset that whereas SRO No. 186 was issued to introduce the individual contours and the periphery of many types of taxable agency services inclusive of shipping agency services each necessarily set apart and categorized under distinct service codes by reference to their unique spheres of operations, the parent statute being the VAT and SD Act sets out a statutory scheme to make certain of these services zero-rated services.. Sections 21(1)(Ka) and 24(11)(Ka) and (Gha) are in that respect the cornerstones of such a scheme. The declarations, therefore, in section 24(11)(Ka) and (Gha) that the supply of services to any "international transport" and "directly connected to the operation or management of an ocean-going ship or an aircraft engaged in international transport" shall be zero-rated connects readily to the rendering of section 2(12) "international transport" services under the statutory scheme. Upon a plain reading of these provisions we can readily deduce, therefore, that whoever performs the activities as mentioned section 24(11)(Ka) and (Gha) read with section 2(12) of the VAT and SD Act shall be entitled to zero-rated VAT. It must not be lost sight of further that the term "shipping agent" does find its pride of place in section 2(a) of the Customs Act, 1969 and that all the varied and various agency services brought by the Customs Act into the definition of the word "agent" in section 2(a) find further elaboration under SRO No. 186 of 2019. 

 24. Predicated on the above, and turning to the explanation provided under Service Code No. 5035.00 in SRO No. 186, this Court finds that the said SRO clearly identifies the function of shipping agents as being limited to arrival, stay and departure of a conveyance (vessel) and that on the other hand services mentioned in section 2(11), that is ancillary transport services, relate broadly to the handling of goods at various stages for port, customs assessment and clearance, storage and transportation purposes, thereby, establishing a fundamental difference between the services classified as ancillary transport services and those rendered by shipping agents in the realm of dealing purely with the vessel or conveyance engaged in international transport. In other words, the petitioners are found to be involved in providing services in matters related to the conveyance itself i.e., the vessel but are not connected directly to dealings in the goods that are transported on these vessels. 

 27. We note further that these other separate categories of services attract VAT at distinct and varied rates according as the separate service codes assigned each of them individually under SRO No. 186. As per SRO No. 186, separate service codes have accordingly been assigned, for example, to Freight Forwarders (5015.10) and C&F Agents (5015.20). Similarly, taxation as per the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 in respect of each such service including shipping agents' services takes place hereunder: 

 28. Predicated on the above, it is found that in view of the clear distinctions drawn in the fiscal (income tax) legal regime between varied categories of services under SRO No. 186 considered in conjunction with the relevant provisions of the VAT and SD Act and the Income Tax Ordinance, the NBR's claim that "shipping agents in many situations are involved with other shipping or export-import related businesses such as freight forwarding agent, or handling agent and storing of goods etc. which makes it really difficult to make a clear distinction of their source of income and to differentiate which portion of their income is purely commission for the services provided as shipping agent (except ancillary transport services)" is simply untenable not permitting of favourable consideration in the realm of fiscal law. Fiscal law's administration, the respondents would do well to bear in mind, demands specificity and precision of categorization of services as above indicated and which the respondents' general assertions above appear wholly to ignore to their own detriment. 

 31. Staying within the confines of the Customs Act, 1969 and in generally accepting the legal basis of Mr Hassan Ariff's submission this Court takes note too of the defined role of shipping agents specified in the said legislation. Indeed, the definition of "international transport" in section 2(12) of the VAT and SD Act, in this Court's view, finds further content in section 2(a) of the Customs Act as clearly identifies shipping agents as falling under the definition of the term "agent" and section 2(g) of the Customs Act which defines "conveyance" as any means of transport such as a vessel, aircraft or vehicle used inter alia for carrying goods. These provisions of the Customs Act once taken to be the contextual basis for a further understanding of the tenor of section 2(12) of the VAT and SD Act leads inescapably to the deduction in this Court's view of providing statutory cover to services rendered by shipping agents at the point of arrival, the period of stay and at the point of departure of any conveyance as includes a shipping vessel. Delving deeper into the actual nature and ambit of such services, and as pleaded by the petitioners expressly as above noted, the petitioners shipping agents in this Court's view can rightfully be viewed as acting in a managerial capacity discharging their respective obligations of oversight and coordination of the activities of all other categories of service providers/agents as also distinctly assigned service codes under SRO No. 186. 

 35. This Court would like to go the extra length to opine further that if the respondents are of mind for the law to operate otherwise then the law awaits amendment or modification to that effect. We are not satisfied that such modification has yet been introduced through an Act of Parliament. This takes us back to the Appellate Division's judgment and order of 29-10-2020 where the apex Court of the land has put a judicial stricture and moratorium on the imposition of VAT on the fees/ commissions of the petitioners shipping agents earned as remuneration in foreign currency from abroad unless the present law is amended by the "Parliament". We are wary of the fact that both the NBR and the BB have conveniently lost sight of this stricture of the highest Court of the land and indeed article 111 of the Constitution in forcing upon all an interpretation of the law aided supposedly by a piece of delegated legislation being SRO No. 186 in particular (and the related SRO No. 188). The respondents are alerted to the fact that any such continued insistence and sustained effort to extract VAT from shipping agents may very well expose the respondents to the risk of allegations of malice in law being resorted to in the application of the law in a manner that runs counter to the proper and reasonable application of the law and the dictates of the highest Court of the land. 

 36. It follows that when SRO No. 186 is intended to serve a limited purpose for delineating services distinctly by assignment of service codes and explanations, there is no excuse for the respondents to fudge and confuse the issue of zero-rated taxable services. The Revenue must aim always to make the underlying scheme of the VAT and SD Act read with the relevant provisions of other laws work and not make these wholly inoperative as has been the case with regard to their actions vis-a-vis the petitioners in the present case. As already above indicated, the respondents must alert themselves to the fact that "exemptions" and "zero-rated VAT" are distinct notions. "Exemptions" as governed by section 126 of the VAT and SD Act are at the end of the day products of administrative decisions either of the government or the NBR subject to limitations and conditions imposed at discretion. Zero-rated VAT status, in contradistinction, is one that is already categorized and entrenched in the statute itself and attaches by express statutory declaration to designated services. This entails a greater compulsion on the respondents collectively taken to follow and strictly apply the letter of the law without resorting to external interpretative tools as has been done in this case unnecessarily and unsuccessfully so. This goes to the very core of the error fundamentally made by the concerned respondents in the issuance of the two impugned orders and which error strikes at the very legality of the two impugned orders. Hence, this Court finds that the two impugned memos dated 1-12-2020 and 29-12-2020 have indeed been passed without lawful authority and from which no legal effect flows. Consequentially, the deduction of VAT on the fees/commission earned by the members of the petitioner No. 1, BSAA including the petitioner Nos. 2-5 from their respective principals from abroad in foreign currency for providing services as shipping agents and, thereby, the refusal to allow the benefit of zero-rated VAT on the aforesaid fees/commission are also declared to be illegal and without lawful authority. Accordingly, the concerned respondents are, hereby, directed to refund any VAT so deducted illegally from the fees/ commission of the petitioners shipping agents within a period of 6(six) weeks computed from the date of receipt of a certified copy of this Judgment and Order.
